chapter_theme: The close of the Sankhya debate: Neelakesi refutes a Lord who is all things and creator, then the pre-existence of effects and the twenty-five principles, and Parasaran concedes and receives right vision.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Sankhya teacher whom Neelakesi debates in the Sankhya sarukkam

766.reading: The opponent holds that because his Lord has the five qualities (dancing, destroying, creating, withdrawing, and the state that shines when release is won), none of the faults Neelakesi has examined touch him.
766.nuance: The five named here are the Saiva five acts, with the dance (ஆடல்) first, though the sarukkam is named for the Sankhya; the verse does not say whether Parasaran now speaks for a lord added to the Sankhya scheme or the debate has turned to a theist. The view is answered at once in 767-775, which is why it is marked refuted.

claims.claim: the Lord who dances, destroys, creates, withdraws and grants release is beyond the faults charged against him

767.reading: Neelakesi answers that if everything spoken proceeds from one being by a single rule, then even the debaters who come forward as others are he, and there is no gain in the dispute; give it up, she says.
767.nuance: The objection turns the debate itself against the doctrine: if the one Lord is all, Parasaran is arguing with himself.

claims.claim: everything that is spoken proceeds from one Lord by one rule
if all is one being, a debate between opponents has no point

768.reading: She asks: if elephants, horses, armies, subjects and everything else are he, then he forever rules only himself, so who could ever say 'this one is our king'?

claims.claim: if all beings are the one Lord, the difference of ruler and ruled vanishes

769.reading: She argues that if all but herself is he, and he destroys, fights and consumes himself, people would have to call him a madman.
769.nuance: பித்தன் (line 4), 'madman', is also a common name of Siva; the verse may be turning the epithet against its bearer, though it does not say so.

claims.claim: a Lord who is everything and destroys his creatures destroys himself, which is madness

770.reading: She compares such a god to a man who stabs his own eye with his own hand, where there is no one else even to ask why, and demands the reason.
770.nuance: The repeated line (1 and 3) makes the image the argument: harm done to creatures by a god who is the creatures has no motive at all.

claims.claim: harm a god who is all things does to beings is harm without reason done to himself

771.reading: She argues that the creator could not have made himself, since before the making he was not, and if another made him there is no end of makers; 'who made you, fool?' she asks.

claims.claim: a creator can neither create himself nor be created without an endless regress of creators

772.reading: She says that penance done after killing upon killing perishes, so that too is unfitting, and a god who makes things after destroying them has no understanding at all and is utterly foolish.
772.nuance: The verse assumes the Jain rule that killing undoes penance and applies it to the god himself; line 3 (இன்றிதின் றிட்டுப் படைப்பின்) is read as destroying before creating.

claims.claim: penance done by one who kills is destroyed by the killing
a god who destroys and then creates shows no wisdom

773.reading: She lists what the one god must be: thinker and speaker, flesh and food, healer and disease, the angry one, the killer and the one who dies, giver and receiver, the one who removes; and asks what he gains by any of it.

claims.claim: a god who is both doer and sufferer of every act gains nothing by acting

774.reading: Neelakesi concludes that the god who bites as the dog, kills as the jackal, beats and eats as the demon, gores as the bull, torments as the fly and stings as the ant is everywhere one evil god.
774.nuance: The catalogue of small cruelties is the Jain's moral test of the doctrine that God is all: whatever harms a living thing would be God harming.

claims.claim: if the one god is every creature, he is the doer of all their harms and so an evil god

775.reading: She asks whether, if this god who burns, dances and destroys with his foot is also the one who creates with his hand, the confusion of fools could ever end.
775.nuance: Lines 1-2 seem to recall deeds told of Siva (a burning, the dance, a foot that destroys, one who did penance), but the words are compressed and the episodes cannot be fixed from them.

claims.claim: a god who both destroys and creates gives no ground for clear understanding

776.reading: Turning to his doctrine that things are eternal, she says he must hold that the tall palm is already in its seed; then however large it is, why not say that much is also in the hand that holds the seed, fool?
776.nuance: The verse attacks the Sankhya teaching that the effect already exists in its cause; the reductio is the Jain's, and Parasaran's own wording of the doctrine is not given.

claims.claim: since things are eternal, the effect already exists in its cause, as the palm in its seed
if the tree were already in the seed, the hand holding the seed would hold the tree

777.reading: When he says the tree is not there now but will be later, she answers that he then makes it non-existent at one time and existent at another, and so all things are both; thus the red-streaked-eyed one set out the truth.
777.nuance: The opponent's retreat ('not now, but later') is taken as granting the Jain position that a thing is existent and non-existent in different respects; the verse ends the satkarya argument by absorbing it.

claims.claim: the effect is not now but exists later
every thing is both existent and non-existent according to its time

778.reading: She says he has spread three things (the formed, the formless and space) into twenty-five, while the formless, the non-world and the insentient are three that belong together of their own right.
778.nuance: அலோகம் (line 3), the space beyond the world, is a Jain category, so she sets her own scheme against his count; line 4 (செருவோ டுரிமையிற் சேர்பவு மன்றே) is hard to construe.

claims.claim: the principles of reality are twenty-five
the formless, the non-world and the insentient are categories of their own

779.reading: She recalls that he said the person who pervades the whole world is real and that primal nature endures, and tells him to learn by the right count that here earth and the other three come first.
779.nuance: Lines 3-4 are obscure; the sense that the four elements are taken as basic is a guess from நிலமுத னான்கே.

claims.claim: the person pervades the whole world, and primal nature lasts

780.reading: She tells him that he, a bound soul, should not take his supreme self alone to be perfected while denying that state and knowledge to souls, since he himself said that self enjoys and sees.
780.nuance: Sankhya's person is inactive yet a seer and enjoyer; Neelakesi takes the two verbs (துய்த்தல், காண்டல்) as admitting what the Jain soul has, knowledge and experience, and so as giving every soul the perfected state.

claims.claim: the supreme self is the one that enjoys and sees
perfection and knowledge belong to every soul, not to one supreme self

781.reading: Parasaran says he has taken this from the jewelled one whose name is her bee-filled hair, and when he says it she tells him he did not know before and now sees, and gives him right vision.
781.nuance: குழற்பெயர் (line 1), 'named for her hair', plays on Neelakesi's name (the dark-haired one). காட்சி is the Jain jewel of right vision, which she gives the defeated as in the earlier sarukkams.
781.event: Parasaran concedes that he has taken Neelakesi's teaching, and she gives him right vision.

782.reading: She tells him to give up the thought that there is no principle beyond the twenty-five, to worship the red feet of the Jina, and to live well.
782.event: Neelakesi bids Parasaran leave the twenty-five principles and worship the Jina's feet.

claims.claim: there is no principle beyond the twenty-five
one should worship the feet of the Jina

links.note: Manimekalai's Sankhya speaker lets primal nature unfold and withdraw by itself and names no creator; in the Neelakesi's Sankhya sarukkam the opponent defends a Lord of five acts, with the dance first.
links.teaches: The two polemical epics give the same school different shapes: the Buddhist account keeps Sankhya godless, while the Jain account hangs a Saiva-style lord on it, so neither can be read alone as what the Tamil Sankhyas held.

links.note: Tirumular makes the five dances the five acts done by grace; the Neelakesi cites the dance and the acts only as the opponent's shield, which 767-775 break.
links.teaches: The doctrine Tirumular offers as the heart of grace is the very one the Jain debater names in order to refute, and her answer (a god who is all is the author of every harm) is the objection Tirumular's dance never meets.

gains.a: the epic's brief list is shown to be a real Saiva teaching, the dance joined to the five acts, not a straw man
gains.b: the verse gains a hostile contemporary reading that treats the five acts as making god responsible for destruction and harm

links.note: The Kural's first couplet says the world has the primal Lord as its first; the Neelakesi argues no creator can be first without an endless regress of makers.
links.teaches: Kural 1 says the Lord is first but never that he made the world, so the Jain regress argument against a creator leaves the couplet standing, which shows why Jain readers could keep it.

gains.a: the epic's attack is shown to be aimed at a maker, not at every claim that a Lord comes first
gains.b: the couplet's simile of the first letter gains a test that sets first apart from creator

links.note: Sivavakkiyar uses the banyan folded in its own seed as the image of Parabrahman grown within a man; Neelakesi mocks the tall palm said to be already in its seed.
links.teaches: The tree-in-the-seed image that a Siddhar offers as an insight was, for a Jain debater, the weak point of the doctrine that effects pre-exist, so one image carries a mystic's claim and a logician's refutation.

gains.a: the epic's reductio is shown to bear on a living image of Tamil devotion, not only on a school's technical thesis
gains.b: the Siddhar's image meets an objection it never answers: if the tree is in the seed, why is the hand that holds the seed not holding a tree

links.note: Against Mokkalan (389) Neelakesi held that a thing's modes perish and arise while the thing stays; against the Sankhya (777) she says a thing is non-existent now and existent later, both at once.
links.teaches: One Jain doctrine is turned two ways: against the Buddhist's momentary things she stresses what lasts, against the Sankhya's lasting effects she stresses what is not yet, and each answer depends on the other.

links.note: Manimekalai's Sankhya speaker calls the person the one awareness that knows all; Neelakesi takes the seer and enjoyer as the opponent's own words and gives that knowing to every soul.
links.teaches: Where the Buddhist epic only records the person as one knowing awareness, the Jain epic uses the same attribute to argue that the Sankhya has already granted a knowing soul in every being.

links.note: With Arkkachandra (264) Neelakesi offered right vision as the path; with Parasaran (781) the defeated man concedes in his own words and she gives him that vision.
links.teaches: The Neelakesi ends its debates with a gift and not only a win: the same jewel of right vision closes the Buddhist and the Sankhya sarukkams, so conversion is the form a victory takes.

new_concepts.gloss: formal debate between schools, opened by a challenge and held before a king's assembly
new_concepts.label_source: the sarukkam's rubric (சாங்கிய வாதச் சருக்கம்); verse 767 has வாதுசெய் வார்கள்

new_concepts.gloss: transformation: a substance passing into new modes, as milk into curd, while it remains
new_concepts.label_source: label from an earlier chapter (386-389); here the argument over the seed and the palm (776-777)

new_concepts.gloss: in Jain teaching an extended existent (astikaya): dharma, adharma, space, matter and souls
new_concepts.label_source: label from an earlier chapter; here the verse's அருவோடு அலோகம் அசேதனம் (778)

source_issues: 772 line 2: the e-text's '•' was repaired to ஃ (அஃதும்).
769 lines 1-2: என்னை யொழித்து ... சொன்ன முறைமையன் is hard to construe.
775 lines 1-2: வெந்துநெஞ் சாண்டிடத் தாடி தவஞ்செய்த is obscure; the episodes alluded to cannot be fixed.
778 line 4: செருவோ டுரிமையிற் சேர்பவு மன்றே is obscure.
779 lines 3-4: எண்முறை யறிமற் றீண்டுபு நன்றன வீறா is obscure, perhaps corrupt.
781 line 3: பண்டே லறியெனப்பராசர runs words together and பண்டேல் is doubtful.
